content: When something breaks and you have to explain
it fast, you say begin, not commence. You say
hide, not conceal. Every plain verb here has
a French twin that came after 1066 and took
the formal jobs; the plain word kept the rest.
begin      commence    the French of the court
buy        purchase    the ledger and the deed
end        conclude    taken whole from Latin
ask        inquire     Old French enquere
The twin is not better, only later. Purchase
belongs on the receipt, buy in the shop. The
plain word is the one you reach for first, and
that is no accident: it has been here longer.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: begin, buy, end, ask.
An adjective in the plain layer names what
the body can feel: deep water, a sharp edge,
a strong arm. Its French twin names the
judgment: a profound thought, an acute mind,
a robust defense. Both are right; they stand
in different rooms.
bold       courageous  Old French corageus
deep       profound    Old French profond
fair       just        Old French juste
strong     robust      Latin robustus, of oak
Fair meant beautiful before it meant just,
and Old English faeger still shows in a fair
face. Robust is oak in Latin, so a strong
case and a robust one are the same tree.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: bold, deep, fair, strong.
The plain words for people are the words of
the hearth: folk, kin, foe, king. The French
twins are the words of the state and the
title: people, relatives, enemy, sovereign.
The lord was Old English hlaford, the keeper
of the loaf; the master came with the court.
foe        enemy       Old French enemi
folk       people      Anglo-French people
king       sovereign   Old French soverain
earl       count       Anglo-French counte
The earl kept his English name after 1066;
the French count survives only in his wife,
the countess. Knight was Old English cniht, a
boy in service, long before it was a rank.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: foe, folk, king, earl.
English builds its abstract nouns from a
plain word and a plain ending: free + dom,
friend + ship, brother + hood, kind + ness.
The French twin comes as one word, taken
whole, and it is the word of the document:
liberty in the law, freedom in the chest.
freedom    liberty     Old French liberte
friendship amity       Old French amitie
kingdom    realm       Old French reaume
hardship   adversity   Old French adversite
Some twins are the same word twice: Latin
frater is brother, mater is mother, pater is
father, so fraternity, maternity and paternity
are the -hood words with their sounds shifted.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: freedom, kingdom, kinship.
For the body, the plain word is what you say
and the Latin twin is what the doctor writes.
You have a belly; the chart says abdomen. You
were carried in a womb; the clinic says
uterus. The Latin word came in whole, and it
was never meant for the kitchen.
belly      abdomen     the anatomist's word
gut        intestine   Old French intestin
shin       tibia       taken whole from Latin
dale       valley      Old French valee
The land keeps the same split. A dale is an
English valley, and the word is still spoken
in the north; heaven stands beside paradise,
earth beside terrain, sea beside ocean.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: belly, womb, dale, heath.
The plain words for feeling are short, or
built on a short root with -ful or -some:
glad, grim, gleeful, mournful, loathsome,
awesome. The twins are the words of the
court and the clinic: mad is what you say,
insane is what the judge writes.
glad       joyful      Old French joy
mad        insane      Latin insanus
hateful    odious      Anglo-French odious
downcast   dejected    Latin for thrown down
Downcast and dejected are the same picture
twice, cast down in English and thrown down
in Latin. Dreary began as bloody, from Old
English dreor, gore, and softened to sad.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: glad, mad, grim, dreary.
The words of the house and the field mostly
have no French twin at all. Stool, roof,
hearth, shelf, yoke, rake, trough: the
Normans took the court and the castle, not
the barn, and nobody replaced the words of
the work. Where a twin exists it is the word
of the menu and the trade.
meal       repast      the word of the table
cloth      fabric      Middle French fabrique
thread     filament    Latin filum, a thread
ditch      trench      Old French trenche
Yarn is spun thread and, in a sailor's phrase,
a long tale. Fabric was first the workshop,
and only later the cloth that came out of it.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: meal, cloth, hearth, plow.
The plain words for speech are the words of
the mouth: tongue, tale, saying, oath. The
twins are the words of the altar and the
bench: language, narrative, proverb, vow. To
bless was to hallow with blood; consecrate
is the Latin the church wrote it in.
oath       vow          Old French vou
tale       narrative    Latin narrare, to tell
spell      incantation  Old French incantacion
tongue     language     Old French langage
Spell was a story or a saying before it was
magic. A tongue is the thing in the mouth and
the speech that comes out of it; language was
the same once, from Latin lingua, the tongue.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: oath, tale, spell, tongue.
The weapons kept their English names: sword,
bow, blade and axe have no French twin at all.
Helm the Normans took from the Germanic and
handed back as helmet, the same word with a
French tail. The law is where the twins live:
the victim says theft, the court says larceny.
theft      larceny     the word of the law
slay       execute     Old French executer
spear      lance       Old French lance
ransack    pillage     Old French pilage
Ordeal was Old English ordal, a trial by fire
or water; tribulation is the French for the
same trial. A truce was good faith, treow,
and armistice is Latin, arms standing still.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: sword, theft, truce, slay.
The plain words for change are the farmer's
and the sailor's: the moon waxes and wanes,
the tide ebbs and floods, the crop blooms and
wilts. The twins are the words of the report:
augment, diminish, recede, flourish, languish.
Both say the same thing. One you can see.
wax        augment     Old French augmenter
wane       diminish    Old French diminuer
flood      deluge      Old French deluge
tide       current     Old French corant
Tide was Old English tid, a time, an hour,
and time and tide once meant the same. Wax,
to grow, survives only in the moon.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: dawn, wax, wane, tide.
